content: Bovine coronavirus (BCV) belongs to the Coronaviridae family, which consists of enveloped, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA viruses characterized by a club-shaped surface. This virus is responsible for causing Calf Enteritis and plays a role in the Enzootic Pneumonia complex in calves. In adult cattle, it can lead to Winter Dysentery. BCV has the ability to infect both domestic and wild ruminants and is distributed globally. The virus is transmitted horizontally, primarily through oro-fecal or respiratory routes. In calves, infection typically occurs between the ages of one week and three months. Gastrointestinal symptoms include severe diarrhea, dehydration, lethargy, reduced weight gain, and loss of appetite. When the respiratory system is affected, calves may exhibit a nasal discharge that ranges from serous to purulent. Secondary bacterial infections can exacerbate the clinical signs. In adult cattle, infections are usually subclinical, except in cases of Winter Dysentery, which predominantly affects housed cattle during the winter months. Winter Dysentery is characterized by severe diarrhea and a marked reduction in milk production during outbreaks. A presumptive diagnosis can be made based on the animal's history and observed clinical signs. A definitive diagnosis of enteric coronavirus infection requires electron microscopy or an ELISA test performed on fecal or tissue samples. For respiratory infections, confirmation is achieved through a direct fluorescent antibody test on nasal washes, which detects the presence of viral antigens. The haemagglutination inhibition test can be employed to identify the specific strain of coronavirus. Treatment for BCV infection is primarily symptomatic.
